concept.name: Z-spread
concept.definition: The constant spread that, when added to each point of the Treasury (or benchmark) spot rate curve, makes the present value of a bond's cash flows equal to its market price. Unlike a nominal spread measured at a single maturity, it accounts for the entire term structure; unlike OAS, it does not adjust for embedded options.
concept.intuition: It is the single number of extra yield the bond must offer at every point along the curve for its promised cash flows to be worth today's price.
concept.mechanics: Each cash flow is discounted at the benchmark spot rate for its maturity plus the spread Z; Z is solved numerically so the discounted cash flows sum to the full (dirty) price. For option-free bonds the Z-spread and OAS coincide; for bonds with embedded options the Z-spread includes compensation for option risk.
concept.formula: P = Σ_t CF_t / (1 + (z_t + Z)/2)^(2t), where P is the full price, CF_t the cash flow at time t, z_t the spot rate at t, and Z the Z-spread (semiannual convention).
concept.failure_modes: For callable or prepayable bonds the Z-spread misattributes option value to credit/liquidity, overstating the option-free spread; it also assumes cash flows are certain, so it is misleading for credit-risky securities near distress.
concept.misconceptions: The 'zero-volatility' name does not mean the bond is riskless; it means the spread is constant and no interest-rate volatility model (option adjustment) is applied.
concept.example: A 3-year bond priced at 104.90 with cash flows of 5, 5, and 105 against spot rates of 2.5%, 2.7%, and 3.0% has a Z-spread of about 0.29% (29 bp).
